story.title: From Ruwi's Typewriters to 192 Million Views: Forty-Five Years Inside the Oman Daily Observer

story.meta_description: From a 50-baisa Ruwi broadsheet in 1981 to 191.95 million digital views, editors and readers recall 45 years of the Oman Daily Observer.

detail.extracted_title: From Ruwi's Typewriters to 192 Million Views: Forty-Five Years Inside the Oman Daily Observer
detail.excerpt: Forty-five years after an eight-page broadsheet rolled off a basement press in Ruwi for fifty baisas, the editors, proofreaders, and lifelong readers of Oman's oldest English daily reflect on how a newsroom changes almost every tool it owns without losing its voice.
detail.article_html:
When Conrad Prabhu walked into the newsroom of the Oman Daily Observer in early 1996, you could hear the stories before you read them. Inside the Oman newspaper building in Ruwi, rows of Remington and Underwood typewriters clattered across the floor. A small bottle of white correction fluid stood beside every editor's hand, and down in the basement directly beneath their shoes, the rotary printing press hummed as the next morning's pages took shape.

Three decades later, the newsroom counts its readership in a very different register. In 2025 alone, the Observer recorded 191.95 million visits and views—98.4 million on its website, alongside 56.8 million on Facebook, 33.2 million on Instagram, and the remainder across X and YouTube. Yet as the newspaper marks 45 years since its founding issue, its anniversary supplement lingers less on algorithms than on a quieter question facing every daily paper on earth: how does a newsroom replace nearly all of its instruments and remain itself?

Eight Pages for Fifty Baisas

The first copy appeared on 15 November 1981 from the Oman press house in Ruwi. It ran eight pages, published Sunday through Thursday, sold for 50 baisas, and carried a masthead promise the paper still keeps: All the News, Every Morning.

For years, change arrived slowly, then all at once. A 16-page color edition debuted in January 1990. A Friday issue joined in November 1997, and in March 1999 the team packed up its desks in Ruwi and moved to Madinat Al Ilam. In August 2020, a Royal Decree dissolved the old press establishment and brought both Oman and the Observer directly under the Ministry of Information.

Dates on a timeline, however, rarely capture the smell of a print room. Mariam Khalfan, who joined as the newspaper's first Omani English-language proofreader before becoming a reporter in 1999, remembers work that was far more physical than clerical. Producing an issue meant slicing paper galleys by hand, pasting columns onto layout boards, loading rolls of bromide paper, and breathing ink and solvent fumes long into the evening before modern presses arrived.

Veteran editor Liju Cherian recalls the days that tested the room's nerve. On 11 September 2001, the team rushed out a four-page early edition in an era when online news was barely in its infancy. When Cyclones Gonu in 2007 and Phet in 2010 washed out roads and flooded neighborhoods across Muscat, many staffers could not reach the building—yet illustrated editions still made it to press to document what the country had lived through. Across four and a half decades, the printing press fell silent for an extended stretch only once: 148 days during the COVID-19 pandemic, under a national Supreme Committee directive.

One Update at Noon, Sent to Students Abroad

The Observer stepped onto the internet in 1997, the very year public internet access reached the Sultanate. By today's habits, the rhythm sounds disarmingly calm: the website was updated once a day, right at twelve noon.

According to Qais bin Abdulrahim Al Salih, one of the founders of that early online desk, the goal had nothing to do with beating competitors to a headline. The team simply wanted Omani embassies and Omani university students studying overseas to have a reliable window onto news from home.

Over the past five years, that modest midday bulletin has grown into a full digital newsroom in a country where 95.3 percent of residents now use the internet. A redesigned website launched in 2021, followed in March 2022 by a dedicated English-language mobile news app, a monthly digital magazine titled The Correspondent, and a weekly newsletter. A WhatsApp channel introduced in 2023 grew past 33,500 subscribers, and in 2026 the digital team established a visual production unit, Observer Studio.

In his anniversary editorial, Editor-in-Chief Abdullah bin Salim Al Shueili noted that keeping a daily newspaper thriving amid smartphones, short-form video, and artificial intelligence is no small feat. While crediting sustained institutional support, he drew a firm line between tools and principles: technology will keep shifting, whereas accuracy, fairness, credibility, and public service are never up for negotiation.

A School Without Classrooms

Ask the people who spent their youth at the copy desk what the paper meant to them, and they speak of it less as an employer than as an apprenticeship. Shaddad Al Musalmi, who spent more than 25 years with the Observer, wrote that he thought he was taking a job at a newspaper and discovered he had enrolled in a school without classrooms—one that taught him to listen to a fisherman in Sur and a minister in Muscat with the exact same measure of respect.

Around the main editorial table sat a miniature portrait of Gulf working life: Omanis, Indians, and Britons arguing over headlines and page proofs together. Badr bin Zahir Al Kiyumi, who arrived as a page designer in 2002 and rose to Deputy Managing Editor, remembers 14-to-16-hour stretches in the building before the first edition rolled out at four in the morning. Managing Editor Mai Al Abri, reflecting on 15 years in the newsroom, observed that citizens and residents in Oman have remained the steady center of their reporting regardless of how stories are delivered.

Outside the newsroom, readers carry their own private history with the broadsheet. British resident Maggie Jeans, who first picked up the paper in 1989, noted how opinion and public discussion have widened alongside social media and digital subscriptions—adding that she still prefers unfolding the print edition in a café. Consultant neonatologist Dr. Manoj Malviya wrote in to propose a standing medical column to push back against health misinformation online.

Perhaps the most enduring tribute came from consultant psychiatrist Dr. Hamad Al Sinawi. Nearly 39 years ago, as a first-year student walking through the library at Sultan Qaboos University, he picked up a copy of the Observer—and never stopped. In an age when anyone holding a phone can call themselves a reporter, he wrote, a room full of editors who verify facts before publishing only grows more precious. He ended his letter with a quiet pact between newspaper and reader: “As long as you keep writing, I will keep reading.”

detail.instagram_caption:
When Conrad Prabhu walked into the newsroom of the Oman Daily Observer in Ruwi in early 1996, the building had its own unmistakable soundtrack: rows of Remington and Underwood typewriters clattering upstairs, bottles of white correction fluid beside every desk, and the printing press rumbling in the basement underfoot.

Forty-five years after its first eight-page issue rolled off the press on 15 November 1981 for 50 baisas, Oman's oldest English-language daily now reaches an audience measured in tens of millions—recording 191.95 million visits and views across its website and social platforms in 2025 alone. Along the way came hand-sliced layout galleys, a 1997 website updated once daily at noon so Omani students abroad could read news from home, Cyclone Gonu print runs when roads were washed out, and 4 a.m. deadlines shared by Omani, Indian, and British editors around one table.

Yet the most lasting measure of those four and a half decades comes from the people shaped by its pages—from veteran reporter Shaddad Al Musalmi, who learned to listen to a fisherman in Sur and a minister in Muscat with equal respect, to psychiatrist Dr. Hamad Al Sinawi, who picked up his first copy in the Sultan Qaboos University library nearly 39 years ago and wrote simply: "As long as you keep writing, I will keep reading."
